notes: Garden Tracker Explore fact & "Did you know?" cards. Text is written in our own words at a simple reading level; facts are checked against the cited extension pages. Photos are PD / CC0 / CC BY / CC BY-SA with credits.

cards.title: Patrick's weed-pulling trick
cards.text: Water the ground first so the soil gets soft. Then hold the weed at the bottom, right next to the ground, and twist as you pull it out.

src.t: Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — Controlling weeds by cultivation or hand pulling
Univ. of Maryland Extension — Manage weeds without chemicals

related.label: Pull weeds when they are small

cards.title: Ladybugs love aphids
cards.text: One grown-up ladybug of a common kind can eat up to 50 aphids in a day. That makes ladybugs great garden helpers!

src.t: Colorado State Univ. Agricultural Biology — Lady beetles

cards.title: Don't eat green potatoes
cards.text: Never eat a potato that is green under the skin. Keep potatoes in a dark place, because light can turn them green.

src.t: Iowa State Univ. Extension AnswerLine — Sprouting or greening potatoes: keep or toss?

cards.title: Squash needs bees
cards.text: Squash plants have boy flowers and girl flowers. A bee must carry pollen from a boy flower to a girl flower to make a squash.

src.t: Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Growing summer squash and zucchini in home gardens

cards.title: How much water do veggies drink?
cards.text: In summer, a veggie garden uses about ¼ inch of water each day. So if you water every 4 days, give it about 1 inch.

src.t: Colorado State Univ. Extension — Irrigating the vegetable garden

cards.title: Rain barrel water is for plants
cards.text: Rain barrel water is not safe to drink, but you can use it on your veggies. Water in the morning, and not on the day you pick.

src.t: Clemson HGIC — Best practices for application of harvested rainwater on edibles

cards.title: How much do bin worms eat?
cards.text: Starting a worm bin with 1 pound of worms? Feed them about 3 pounds of food scraps each week.

src.t: Cornell Waste Management Institute — Six easy steps to setting up a worm bin

cards.title: Hungry red wigglers
cards.text: A red wiggler worm can eat about its own weight in old food every day! Use red wigglers in a worm bin, because garden worms can't live there.

src.t: Oregon State Univ. Extension EM 9034 — Composting with worms

cards.title: Deer jump high
cards.text: Deer can jump very high. To keep them out of the garden, a fence should be at least 6 to 8 feet tall.

cards.title: Don't pick frozen greens
cards.text: Do not pick cool-season crops like kale while they are frozen. Wait for them to thaw, which is often by late morning.

src.t: Iowa State Univ. Yard & Garden — Using low tunnels to extend the season

cards.title: Food garden or herb garden?
cards.text: A food garden grows plants you eat as a meal, like beans, squash and tomatoes. It needs more room than an herb garden.

src.t: Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Planting the vegetable garden
Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Growing herbs

cards.title: What is an herb garden?
cards.text: An herb garden grows small plants that add flavor, like basil, dill and parsley. It fits in a small spot or in pots with holes in the bottom.

src.t: Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Growing herbs

cards.title: Why grow both kinds?
cards.text: Food plants fill your plate. Herbs make food taste great, and you pick just a few leaves at a time.

src.t: Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Growing herbs

cards.title: Herbs love sun too
cards.text: Herbs and food plants both like sun. Most herbs want 6 or more hours of sun each day.

src.t: Univ. of Minnesota Extension — Growing herbs

cards.title: Pull weeds from damp soil
cards.text: Weeds slide out easier when the soil is damp. Hold the weed low, near the ground, and pull slowly to get the root.

related.label: Pull weeds when they are small

cards.title: Pull weeds while small
cards.text: Pull weeds when they are tiny. A big weed can make thousands of seeds, and those seeds can cause trouble for years.

related.label: Pull weeds when they are small

cards.title: Mulch stops weeds
cards.text: Spread straw or other mulch 2 to 4 inches deep around your plants. It helps stop weeds and keeps the soil moist.

cards.title: Weed seeds can sleep
cards.text: Some weed seeds can rest in the soil for many years. Digging brings them up to the light, and then they wake up and sprout!

related.label: Cardboard sheet-mulch bed with drip & plant-through holes

cards.title: Wear gloves to weed
cards.text: Put on gloves before you pull weeds. Some weeds are prickly, and some have sap that can bother your skin.

cards.title: One inch a week
cards.text: A garden needs about 1 inch of water each week. Rain counts too, so use a rain gauge to keep track.

cards.title: Measure with a tuna can
cards.text: Set an empty tuna can under your sprinkler. When the water in the can is 1 inch deep, your garden got its weekly drink.

cards.title: Check before you water
cards.text: Poke your finger into the soil. If it is dry two inches down, it is time to water.

cards.title: Water roots in the morning
cards.text: Water early in the day and aim at the soil, not the leaves. Leaves that stay wet at night can get sick.

cards.title: An inch is a lot!
cards.text: One inch of water on a 10-by-10-foot garden is about 62 gallons. That is around twelve big 5-gallon buckets!

cards.title: Deep drinks, deep roots
cards.text: Give plants a slow, deep drink instead of a tiny sip each day. Deep water helps roots grow long and strong.

cards.title: Some roots stay short
cards.text: Lettuce and radishes have short roots, so they dry out fast. Tomatoes and pumpkins push their roots much deeper.

cards.title: Drip saves water
cards.text: Drip hoses drip water right onto the soil near roots. They waste less water than sprinklers.

cards.title: Mix greens and browns
cards.text: Compost needs greens, like fruit scraps and grass, and browns, like dry leaves. Use 2 or 3 scoops of browns for every scoop of greens.

cards.title: Damp like a sponge
cards.text: Keep your compost pile as damp as a squeezed-out sponge. Too wet and it gets smelly; too dry and it slows down.

cards.title: Keep meat out of compost
cards.text: Do not put meat, dairy, or greasy food in a backyard compost pile. Fruit and veggie scraps are great instead.

cards.title: Compost piles get hot!
cards.text: Tiny living things called microbes eat the scraps in a compost pile. They can make the middle heat up to 130-140°F!

cards.title: Stinky compost? Add browns
cards.text: If compost smells like strong cleaning spray (ammonia), it has too many greens. Mix in dry leaves or paper.

cards.title: Worms are soil helpers
cards.text: Some earthworms dig tunnels six feet deep! Worm poop, called castings, helps hold soil together.

cards.title: The wood wide web
cards.text: Under the ground, fungus threads link plant roots together. They trade food with plants and can pass along warnings about bugs.

cards.title: The squeeze test
cards.text: Squeeze a handful of soil into a ball. If it falls apart when you poke it, the soil is ready to dig.

cards.title: Don't dig wet soil
cards.text: Wait to dig or till until the soil is not wet. Digging wet soil packs it into hard, lumpy clods.

cards.title: Fall leaves are treasure
cards.text: Don't throw away fall leaves! Run a lawn mower over them to chop them up, then use them as free mulch.

cards.title: Test your soil
cards.text: A soil test shows what plant food your soil already has. Then you won't add extra food it doesn't need.

related.label: How to take a soil test

cards.title: How deep to plant seeds
cards.text: A good rule: plant a seed about twice as deep as it is wide. A seed 1/4 inch wide goes 1/2 inch deep.

related.label: How deep to plant a seed

cards.title: Toughen up baby plants
cards.text: Before moving seedlings outside, set them out a little longer each day for 1 to 2 weeks. A cold frame is a great spot for this.

cards.title: Soak beet seeds first
cards.text: Beet seeds are hard. Garden experts say to soak them in water for one day before you plant them.

cards.title: Mix carrot seeds with sand
cards.text: Carrot seeds are so tiny! Mix them with a little sand so they spread out, and keep them damp until they sprout.

cards.title: Some seeds need light
cards.text: Some tiny seeds need light to sprout. Sprinkle them on top of the soil, pat them down gently, and keep them damp.

cards.title: Plant tomatoes deep
cards.text: Bury a tomato plant deep, up to its lowest leaves. New roots grow along the buried stem and make the plant strong.

cards.title: Snip, don't pull
cards.text: When seedlings are too crowded, snip the extras at the soil with scissors. Pulling them can hurt the roots of the ones you keep.

photo.by: Dwight Sipler from Stow, MA, USA
photo.title: Snip, don't pull

src.t: Ohio State University Farm to School

cards.title: Start small
cards.text: A small garden is easier to care for. Start with a few easy plants, then grow your garden bigger each year.

cards.title: Keep mint in a pot
cards.text: Mint spreads fast with roots that creep under the ground. Grow it in its own pot so it won't take over.

cards.title: Marigolds vs. tiny worms
cards.text: Marigold roots can fight tiny worms that hurt veggie roots. Grow a thick patch of them in a bed for two months before the veggies go in.

cards.title: Beans feed the soil
cards.text: Beans have tiny helpers living on their roots. They pull nitrogen, a plant food, out of the air!

cards.title: Veggies love sunshine
cards.text: Most vegetables need 6 to 8 hours of sun a day. Plant them in the sunniest spot you have.

cards.title: Greens handle some shade
cards.text: Leafy greens like lettuce and spinach can grow with only a few hours of sun. Most other veggies want at least 6 hours.

cards.title: Young sunflowers follow the sun
cards.text: Sunflowers turn their faces to follow the sun across the sky. They do it by growing a little more on one side of the stem!

cards.title: Cool crops and warm crops
cards.text: Carrots and radishes like cool weather. Tomatoes, peppers, and squash need warm days to grow well.

cards.title: Baby ladybugs love aphids
cards.text: A baby ladybug can eat 200 to 500 aphids as it grows up. It looks like a tiny bug alligator!

cards.title: Lacewing babies eat aphids
cards.text: Baby lacewings are hungry hunters. One can eat up to 200 aphids in a week!

photo.by: Katja Schulz from Washington, D. C., USA
photo.title: Lacewing babies eat aphids

cards.title: Leave the hornworm with white bumps
cards.text: See a hornworm with little white bumps on its back? Leave it, because tiny helper wasps grow there and will hunt more hornworms.

photo.title: Leave the hornworm with white bumps

lesson.label: Pick big bugs off by hand

cards.title: Knock beetles into soapy water
cards.text: Japanese beetles drop down when you bump them. Hold a cup of soapy water under the leaf and tap it.

lesson.label: Pick big bugs off by hand

cards.title: Protect the good bugs
cards.text: Many bug sprays kill good bugs, like ladybugs, along with the pests. Use sprays only when you really need them.

cards.title: Cover squash plants
cards.text: Light row covers over young squash plants keep squash vine borer moths away. Take them off when flowers open so bees can visit.

lesson.label: Stretch the season: row covers and cold frames

cards.title: Thank a pollinator
cards.text: Bees, bats, and butterflies carry pollen from flower to flower. That helps make about one of every three bites we eat!

cards.title: Monarchs need milkweed
cards.text: Monarch caterpillars eat just one kind of plant: milkweed. Grow milkweed to help them!

photo.by: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service - Midwest Region
photo.title: Monarchs need milkweed

cards.title: Bees that buzz
cards.text: Bumble bees hold on to tomato flowers and buzz very fast. The shaking makes the pollen fall out!

cards.title: A flower helped by termites
cards.text: One rare orchid grows and blooms under the ground in Australia. It is the only plant we know that gets help from termites to make seeds!

cards.title: Pick sweet corn in the morning
cards.text: Pick sweet corn early in the morning. Poke a kernel: if the juice looks milky, it is ready!

photo.title: Pick sweet corn in the morning

cards.title: Pick zucchini small
cards.text: Pick zucchini while it is small and tender. Big ones left on the plant slow down new zucchini.

cards.title: Pick veggies young
cards.text: Pick beans, cucumbers, and okra while they are young. They often taste best before they get big.

cards.title: Pinch basil flowers
cards.text: Pinch off basil flower buds as soon as you see them. This keeps the leaves tasting their best.

cards.title: Asparagus needs patience
cards.text: Do not pick asparagus in its first year. Give the young plant time to settle in before you harvest.

cards.title: Hybrid seeds surprise you
cards.text: Seeds from hybrid plants won't grow plants just like the parent. Save seeds from open-pollinated kinds instead.

cards.title: Store seeds cool and dry
cards.text: Keep saved seeds in a sealed glass jar in a cool, dry place like the fridge. Write the name and date on them.

cards.title: Tomato seeds take a bath
cards.text: To save tomato seeds, put the seeds and goo in a jar of water for a few days. Good seeds sink, so rinse and dry them.

cards.title: Listen for the rattle
cards.text: Leave some bean pods on the plant until they are brown and dry. When the seeds rattle inside, they are ready to save.

cards.title: Surprise squash!
cards.text: Zucchini and pumpkins can mix when bees carry pollen. That is why odd squash can pop up in a compost pile!

photo.by: Darya Pino from San Francisco, USA
photo.title: Surprise squash!

cards.title: Milk powder keeps seeds dry
cards.text: Wrap a spoonful of dry milk powder in a tissue and put it in your seed jar. It soaks up wet air.

cards.title: Clean your clippers
cards.text: Wipe your clippers with rubbing alcohol after you cut a sick plant. This helps keep germs from going to other plants.

cards.title: Keep a garden journal
cards.text: Write down what you plant, when it blooms, and when you pick it. Next year you will remember what worked.

cards.title: Clean, dry tools last
cards.text: Brush dirt off tools and dry them before putting them away. Dry tools don't rust as fast.

src.t: UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County

cards.title: Radishes grow fast
cards.text: Radishes sprout fast and are ready to pick in just a few weeks. Kids love growing them!

cards.title: Sunflower growing contest
cards.text: Plant a few kinds of sunflowers and measure them each week. Which one grows tallest?

src.t: NC State Extension Grow For It

cards.title: Plant a senses garden
cards.text: Grow plants to touch and smell, like fuzzy lamb's ear and lavender. A senses garden is fun for the whole family.

cards.title: A plant that rattles
cards.text: False indigo makes seed pods that dry out. When the wind blows, they shake and rattle like toys!

cards.title: Flowers you can eat
cards.text: You can eat nasturtium and pansy flowers! Always ask an adult first, since some plants are poison.

cards.title: A tomato is a berry
cards.text: A tomato is a fruit, not a vegetable. In fact, plant experts say it is a kind of berry!

cards.title: Tomatoes went to court
cards.text: In 1893, the top court in the United States said a tomato is a vegetable for tax rules. Plant experts still say it is a fruit!

cards.title: Tomato's family
cards.text: A tomato is a cousin of the potato and the pepper. They are all in one plant family!

cards.title: Carrots used to be purple
cards.text: The first carrots that farmers grew were purple and yellow. Orange ones came along a long time later!

photo.by: Arnold Gatilao from Oakland, CA, USA
photo.title: Carrots used to be purple

cards.title: Seeds on the outside
cards.text: A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside! Each tiny dot is really a little fruit with one seed inside.

cards.title: One silk, one kernel
cards.text: Every strand of corn silk is tied to one kernel. Pollen must land on each silk to fill the whole ear.

cards.title: The Three Sisters
cards.text: Native American farmers grew corn, beans, and squash together. Corn holds up the beans, and squash leaves shade out weeds.

cards.title: Beets in an ancient garden
cards.text: Beets are very old! A writing from about 800 BC says beets grew in the famous Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

cards.title: Beet juice hair dye
cards.text: Long ago in Britain, some people used beet juice to dye their hair red!

cards.title: Biggest living thing
cards.text: The biggest living thing on land may be a fungus in Oregon! It spreads under about 2,384 acres and may be 2,400 years old.

cards.title: Mushrooms are not plants
cards.text: Mushrooms are not plants! Scientists found that fungi are more like animals than plants.

cards.title: Mushrooms that glow
cards.text: Over 110 kinds of fungi glow in the dark! The glow may draw in bugs that carry their spores.

cards.title: Mushroom muscles
cards.text: Puffball mushrooms fill up with water as they grow. They can push so hard that they lift up stones in a path!

cards.title: Flowers that bloom underground
cards.text: Some rare orchids in Australia live their whole lives under the ground. They even bloom down there!

photo.by: Photographs (a–d) by Etienne Delannoy; (e) by Jeremy Bougoure
photo.title: Flowers that bloom underground

cards.title: So many orchids
cards.text: There are about 28,000 kinds of orchids! They grow on every big land on Earth but one, cold Antarctica.

cards.title: Tuck plants in on frosty nights
cards.text: If frost is coming, cover tender plants with an old sheet or blanket for the night. It traps warmth coming up from the ground.

photo.title: Tuck plants in on frosty nights

lesson.label: Tuck plants in on a frosty night

cards.title: Wait after the last frost
cards.text: Tomatoes do not like the cold. Wait about two weeks after your last frost date to plant them outside.

cards.title: Plant garlic in fall
cards.text: Plant garlic cloves in fall, pointy end up. They sit in the ground all winter and are ready to dig the next summer.

photo.by: Dwight Sipler from Stow, MA, USA
photo.title: Plant garlic in fall

cards.title: Some plants like a little frost
cards.text: Some cool-weather crops can handle a light frost. Some even get better after one!

photo.by: Tracy from North Brookfield, Massachusetts, USA
photo.title: Some plants like a little frost

cards.title: Plant a second garden
cards.text: Lettuce, spinach, and radishes like cool days. Plant them again at the end of summer for a fall crop.

cards.title: Leave stems for bees
cards.text: This fall, leave some dead flower stems standing. Mason bees and other wild bees use hollow stems as safe homes for their babies.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Consider pollinators during fall garden cleanup

cards.title: Bumble bee queens sleep underground
cards.text: In fall, the old bumble bee nest dies. Only new queens live, and they sleep about 10 inches under the ground until spring!

src.t: Ohio State Univ. Extension (Ohioline) — Bumble Bees in Ohio

cards.title: Tuck strawberries in with straw
cards.text: After a few fall frosts, cover your strawberry plants with 3 to 4 inches of straw. Do it before the nights get down to 20°F.

cards.title: Plant spring bulbs in fall
cards.text: Plant tulip and daffodil bulbs in fall, any time before the ground freezes. Set each bulb with its pointy end up.

src.t: Illinois Extension — How to plant flower bulbs for a colorful spring display

cards.title: A weed that sprouts in fall
cards.text: Chickweed sprouts in the fall and stays green all winter. In spring it blooms with tiny white flowers and makes seeds.

photo.title: A weed that sprouts in fall

src.t: University of Maryland Extension — Chickweeds: identification and management

related.label: Pull weeds when they are small

cards.title: Short days slow plants down
cards.text: When days have less than 10 hours of light, plants almost stop growing. This time is called the Persephone Period.

src.t: N.C. Cooperative Extension (NC State) — Persephone Period for planning winter produce

cards.title: Drain hoses before winter
cards.text: Before hard freezes, unhook hoses from outdoor faucets and drain the water out. Store them in a dry, sheltered spot until spring.

src.t: Illinois Extension — How to winterize outdoor plumbing: irrigation, hoses, spigots

cards.title: Grow paperwhites indoors
cards.text: Paperwhite bulbs do not need a cold winter to bloom. Set them on pebbles in a bowl, and keep the water just touching the bulb bottoms.

src.t: Illinois Extension — How to grow and care for paperwhites

cards.title: Logs in a raised bed
cards.text: In a deep raised bed, lay logs, then branches and twigs, then leaves, soil, and compost. As the wood rots, add more compost to keep it full.

src.t: Clemson Univ. Extension HGIC — Hügelkultur Gardening

cards.title: Buried wood holds water
cards.text: Wood buried under a garden bed slowly rots. As it does, it holds water like a sponge and adds food to the soil.

src.t: South Dakota State Univ. Extension — Gardening in Raised Beds and Containers in the Northern Great Plains

cards.title: Let a log bed rest
cards.text: Build a log bed in fall and let it sit a few months. Then the rotting wood will not steal nitrogen, a plant food, from your crops.

src.t: UC Master Gardeners of San Mateo & San Francisco (UC ANR) — Hugelculture

cards.title: Wood to keep out of beds
cards.text: Keep black walnut, black cherry, and treated wood out of a log bed. Cedar rots very slowly, so use just a bit.

photo.title: Wood to keep out of beds

src.t: UC Master Gardeners of San Mateo & San Francisco (UC ANR) — Hugelculture

cards.title: Test old seeds first
cards.text: Fold 10 old seeds in a damp paper towel, put it in a bag, and keep it warm. If only a few sprout, buy new seeds.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Are my seeds still good? Testing seed germination

related.label: How deep to plant a seed

cards.title: Seeds that need winter
cards.text: Milkweed seeds will not sprout until they freeze and thaw all winter. That is why fall is the best time to plant them!

src.t: Illinois Dept. of Natural Resources — Growing Common Milkweed Plants from Seeds

cards.title: Leave a stem on pumpkins
cards.text: Cut pumpkins off the vine with clippers and leave 3 to 4 inches of stem. Pumpkins with no stem don't keep as long.

cards.title: Brussels sprouts like frost
cards.text: Brussels sprouts taste best after frosty weather. The bottom sprouts get ready first, so pick from the bottom up.

src.t: University of Maryland Extension — Growing Brussels Sprouts in a Home Garden

cards.title: Fall colors were hiding
cards.text: Leaves have yellow and orange hiding under the green. When fall nights get long, the green fades and the hidden colors show!

src.t: USDA Forest Service — The Joy and Science of Fall Colors

cards.title: Wash pots before reusing
cards.text: Scrub old pots in soapy water, then soak them 10 minutes in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water and rinse. Wear gloves with bleach.

src.t: Iowa State Univ. Extension — How to Clean and Disinfect Plant Containers
